Named after its original Ibanez catalog number, this olive-green stompbox from 1979 has been praised, mythologized, and misattributed for forty-five years running. Collectors pay four hundred dollars for a vintage original when a reissue sits on the shelf for $170 new. Whole forum threads collapse under the weight of op-amp chip debates. And the guitarist most often credited with making the pedal famous—the one whose name is spoken in the same breath as the TS808 everywhere from gear shops to boutique pedal forums—mostly used a different model. None of that diminishes the sound, which remains one of the most distinctive and widely imitated in rock and blues history. But it does mean the TS808’s real story is considerably more interesting than its mythology. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO How to Get the Tone ↓ Where It Started: The Tube Screamer Is Born 1979. The overdrive pedal was still a fairly new idea. Boss had just released the OD-1, Electro-Harmonix was selling the Big Muff, and the MXR Distortion+ had been available since 1973. Then Nisshin Co.—a Japanese manufacturer better known for guitar pickups than effect pedals—developed an entirely different approach to overdrive for Ibanez’s effects catalog. Rather than clipping a signal into hard, buzzing fuzz-adjacent distortion, the circuit used an op-amp-based soft clipper to push a signal into the warm, vocal, midrange-heavy zone that sits between a clean tone and a fully crunch-saturated one. That pedal launched as the Ibanez TS808 Tube Screamer Overdrive Pro, and it changed how guitarists thought about what an overdrive pedal was supposed to do. Nisshin Co.—now far better known under its own Maxon brand name—manufactured the Tube Screamer for Ibanez throughout the original production run from 1979 to 1981. The TS808 was discontinued when Ibanez updated the design into the TS9 in 1982, with the TS10 Tube Screamer Classic following later in the decade. The TS808 reissue arrived around 1996 and has been in continuous production since, manufactured in Japan to the original specification. In 2024, Ibanez marked the 45th anniversary with a limited sapphire-blue housing edition—confirmation that the TS808 still carries serious brand weight after four and a half decades in the market. The circuit’s architecture is deceptively simple. At its core is an op-amp gain stage with soft clipping diodes in the feedback loop.
